activities.caption: same two sounds, different languages, different fates
activities.name: poRelBuckets

config.prompt: An inventory is a fact about a language — file each case:
buckets: merged in English — one phoneme here, split or used elsewhere

items.label: sip/zip, cat/bat, light/right — swap the sound, swap the meaning
Hindi's dental versus retroflex t — two phonemes there; English hears one
p versus b for Arabic speakers — borrowings with p come out as b, and the difference sounds alien rather than meaningful
Thai's aspirated p — contrastive there; English treats both p-sounds as one

config.why: About 24 consonants and around 20 vowels — roughly 44, a middling count: the inventory is about the language's organisation, not the sounds themselves.

activities.anchor: The same phoneme is pronounced differently depending on its environment
activities.caption: pair each environment with the costume it gets
activities.name: poAlloMatch

config.prompt: The phoneme is the character; allophones are the costumes — pair them:

pairs.left: /p/ at the start of a stressed syllable ('pin', 'attack')

pairs.right: clear l — front of tongue raised
dark l — back of tongue raised

config.why: The aspiration rule is exceptionless across the lexicon and applied every second — yet no speaker can state it.

activities.anchor: This single distinction explains most of what foreign accents are
activities.caption: diagnose two sounds — walk the decision
activities.name: poDiagnoseBranch

config.root: Fieldwork: an unwritten language, two sounds on tape. What are they to each other?

start.text: Swapping one sound for the other sometimes changes a word's meaning — unpredictably. Verdict?

choices.label: Contrastive — separate phonemes
choices.feedback: Meaning-differences that resist prediction are the phoneme signature.

choices.label: The difference tracks position — one only ever appears before a stressed vowel

phoneme.text: Separate phonemes — the contrast lives in the inventory. But the two sounds are acoustically very similar; does that matter?

choices.label: Ask what the ear alone can decide

allophone.text: Allophones — the costume, not the character. A learner's native system will transfer: producing these where the target language has phonemes.

choices.label: But no minimal pair exists for them anywhere — now what?

ear.text: Acoustic distance misleads: clear and dark l differ dramatically yet are allophones, while Hindi's dental and retroflex t are acoustically close and are separate phonemes. Contrast, not similarity, decides.

fieldwork.text: Most contrasts in most languages lack a perfect pair — fall back on patterned distribution: patient word lists, and the wug test run in reverse on an adult system.

config.why: Contrast versus predictability decides; the ear alone misleads — and accent transfer falls straight out of it: allophones where the target language has phonemes.

activities.caption: find the line the rule refuses
activities.name: poPluralSpot

config.prompt: One line of this plural report is wrong — click it:
lines: After voiceless sounds the ending is [s]: cats, books.
After voiced sounds it is [z]: dogs, pens.
After sibilants it is [ɪz]: buses, judges.
You memorise the ending word by word.
Children overapply the rule ('foots', 'goed') before settling on the exceptions.
config.correction: Nobody memorised it per word — the rule assigns by the final sound across the whole lexicon, nonsense words included ('the plural of blork is blorks').
config.why: Overapplication is the fingerprint of a rule at work — the same logic the wug test made famous.

config.prompt: Japanese syllables are almost strictly consonant-plus-vowel; English permits three-consonant onsets ('strength') and a four-consonant coda (/strɛŋkθs/). How many consonants does Hawaiian's entire phonology run?
config.why: Eight consonants and five vowels, with syllables that never end in a consonant — legality lines each language draws for itself, which is why 'bnick' sounds impossible and 'Klaxon' feels native.
config.context: Phonotactics can be stated precisely enough to program — and loanwords get forced through it ('sutoraiku' for strike).

activities.caption: pair each process with its giveaway
activities.name: poConnectedMatch

config.prompt: Rule-governed interactions — pair the process with its example:

pairs.right: assimilation — the sound copies its neighbour's features
deletion — sounds vanish in fast speech, predictably
epenthesis — an insertion repairs an illegal sequence

pairs.left: written transcriptions of real speech always look wrong
pairs.right: the ear cleans up what the mouth did — perception runs through the phoneme layer

config.why: All three run automatically, below awareness — evidence that perception is organised, not raw.

activities.anchor: Accent differences are phonological rules set differently
activities.caption: drag the divider — one rule, two settings
activities.name: poAccentCompare

config.prompt: Rhoticity — the same grammar, different settings — drag the divider:

before.label: Rhotic — most American and Irish accents
before.text: 'Car' keeps its r-sound before consonants — one rule, switched on.

after.label: Non-rhotic — most English and Australian accents
after.text: The r is deleted before consonants — the same rule, switched off. Mergers ('cot'/'caught' collapsing into one vowel, spreading right now) and th-fronting ('fink' for 'think') are more settings, not sloppiness.

config.why: Because rules are systematic, accents are mutually intelligible systems with predictable maps of difference — the same machinery that ran the Great Vowel Shift, rule by rule.

activities.anchor: organises English phonology more than anything visible in spelling
activities.caption: true or false — the hidden organiser
activities.name: poStressJudge

statements.s: 'INsult' the noun versus 'inSULT' the verb — stress alone fixes the meaning.
statements.why: Nouns and verbs borrowed as pairs swap stress; no letters change.

statements.s: Vowels reduce to schwa when unstressed — 'photograph' versus 'photography' has the same letters and different vowels.
statements.why: The stress moved, so the vowels followed.

statements.s: English is syllable-timed: every syllable gets an even slice of time.
statements.why: English is stress-timed — stressed syllables land at roughly even intervals while unstressed ones crowd between.

statements.s: The aspiration of 'pin' appears word-initially before a stressed vowel — stress conditions the allophones.
statements.why: The rule's environment is stated in stress terms.

statements.s: Second-language learners rarely need to add English stress consciously.
statements.why: It is the feature learners most often have to add consciously — the rhythm they hear as the language's music.
